acceptance.check: In the demo budget with a report filtered on `category contains %%%%%%Z`, the category axis keeps every category and the page stays interactive throughout — no spinner that outlives the settle, and no frozen table that needs a reload. What the browser falsifies is that a heavy wildcard value is handled at all rather than hanging, and that the axis stays intact; the falsifiable structural form of the timing claim is AC-8.

acceptance.check: The bound is the measured one, pinned on BOTH sides of the boundary: a raw pattern of more than 4 unescaped `%`/`?` wildcards is refused and one of exactly 4 is accepted (`%%%%` compiles, `%%%%%` returns null); a pattern longer than 256 characters is refused and one of exactly 256 compiles. This is the falsifiable form of IAC-1's timing claim, since the demo budget is too small to exhibit the hang.

acceptance.check: The query side is paired with the axis, and the pairing is stated per operator rather than as a slogan. `unicodeLike` returns 1 for a refused pattern. validated_work_order.approach:
Put the bound inside `likePatternToRegex` and make its refusal explicit in the type. Two module-private constants — `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH = 256` and `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS = 4` — are checked before compiling and inside the compile loop respectively. The counter increments only on the unescaped `%` and `?` branches, never on the escaped branch, so `\%` costs 0 and a `contains` of `\%` (pattern `%\%%`) costs 2. Over-long patterns are refused before any regex is constructed. On refusal the function returns `null` instead of a `RegExp`, which pushes the direction question to every call site in the type system rather than leaving it to a default.

The cap of 4 is what the measurement supports and it changes nothing a user can currently observe: running the counter over every value any existing test pins gives a maximum of 3 (`contains '%'`, `contains '?'`, `contains 'o%'` all compile to 3), so the accepted region is untouched. The exact boundary pair for QA is `%%oo` (pattern `%%%oo%`, exactly 4, accepted, narrows to Food) and `%%oo%` (pattern `%%%oo%%`, exactly 5, refused, keeps all 21) — adjacent in the input, 4 against 5, neither degenerate. The same pair for the raw-pattern unit test is `%%%%` against `%%%%%`. The length boundary pair is a 254-character value (pattern length exactly 256, accepted) against a 255-character value (pattern length 257, refused).

Every consumer then refuses OPENLY, which is the money invariant. Two surfaces, stated separately because they are genuinely different:

On the REPORT AXIS (budgetDataQuery.ts, pure JS over `CategoryEntity.name`, typed `string`, no SQL NULL in play): `contains` keeps a category when `matcher === null || matcher.test(text)` and `doesNotContain` keeps one when `matcher === null ? true : !matcher.test(text)`. The second is the one that bites — negating a match-everything result would drop every category and reintroduce the money bug fixed in PR #9.

On the QUERY / RULES side (unicodeLike returns 1 for a cached `null`), the effect is inherited from the SQL the compiler already emits, so it is worth stating precisely rather than as a slogan:
  - `$like` (compiler.ts:733-735) emits `UNICODE_LIKE(pat, NORMALISE(left))` with no NULL disjunct, so a refusal returns 1 and matches EVERY transaction, including rows whose column is NULL (`NORMALISE(NULL)` is NULL, unicodeLike coerces a null value to `''` at unicodeLike.ts:12, and the refusal short-circuits before any `.test()`).
  - `$notlike` (compiler.ts:741-743) emits `(NOT UNICODE_LIKE(pat, NORMALISE(left)) OR left IS NULL)`, so a refusal makes `NOT 1` = 0 and a row qualifies EXACTLY WHEN `left IS NULL` — no transaction for a non-nullable column, and precisely the NULL-valued rows for a nullable one. On the rules path `left` is nullable for every field `doesNotContain` accepts (`notes` and `imported_payee` are `f('string')` with no `required` in the AQL schema; `payee` resolves to `payees.name` through a LEFT JOIN). On the report's own category filter the same applies to a transaction with no category.

Both outcomes are subsets of 'everything', so under no operator can the axis end up narrower than what the query returned — which is the defect class fixed in PR #9, and the reason a naive 'return no match' refusal would be a money bug rather than a robustness win. The claim is deliberately NOT 'a refused doesNotContain matches no transaction': that is true only where the column is non-nullable, and it is false for `notes`, which is the field the existing sibling test uses and the one the fixture holds a NULL for.

spending-spreadsheet.ts's direct call to `filterCategoriesByConditions` inherits the axis direction for free, because on refusal the filter keeps every category and its `$oneof` is then a superset of the result set.

Three smaller pieces come along because the change makes their exports dead or their comments incomplete. `canNarrowAxisByConditions` is unexported: it has exactly one caller (:137) and no test imports it (grep across packages/ returns two hits, both in budgetDataQuery.ts), with the reason recorded next to it, satisfying IAC-6's first branch. `REGEX_SPECIAL` loses its `export` for the same reason — its only in-repo uses are likePattern.ts:14, :25 and :35. The `// ? added here` scar is deleted while `// escaped wildcard - treat as literal character` stays. The two comments at :115-125 and :148-153 are NOT rewritten; they describe the three identity early returns accurately today and continue to after this change, and the new sentence added to the second says only what is genuinely different about a refusal — it is not an early return, so the grouped array is rebuilt and an already-empty group is dropped.
assumptions: The demo budget is reached via 'Don't use a server' then 'View demo', which runs createTestBudget (mocks/budget.ts:746) and creates 16 categories in 3 groups (8 Usual Expenses, 5 Bills, 3 Income); the QA setup step adds 2, for 18, and does not add a group, so Split:Group stays 3 + 1.
`add category` in the budget sidebar saves as the user types, so no explicit Save click is needed.
The report under test is the Custom report (Reports > Custom report), reached from the report sidebar's filter control.

`getNormalisedString` is applied to the pattern on BOTH sides before it reaches `likePatternToRegex` — budgetDataQuery.ts:249-250 wraps and normalises, and aql/compiler.ts:734 normalises before emitting UNICODE_LIKE — so the length and wildcard counts agree between the axis and the query and a pattern cannot be refused on one side only.

Every wildcard and length figure quoted in this plan and in qa_script comes from running the counter that will live in likePattern.ts over the wrapped pattern, not from hand-counting. The run that produced them is reproduced in AC-8's how_to_verify, so the implementer can re-derive rather than trust.

alternatives_considered.approach: Memoise the compiled regex (extend the existing LRU in unicodeLike to the report axis too).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It does not address the defect. The epic measured it: 200 compiles of one pattern total under a millisecond while testing it against real names costs minutes, so essentially all of the cost is in `.test()`. The issue body also lists memoisation-whose-only-purpose-is-recompiling as out of scope. (Memoisation is still worth keeping for the refused case, so it is retained — that is a different reason and AC-10 pins it.)

alternatives_considered.approach: Bound the number of wildcards at each call site instead of inside the helper (a cap in budgetDataQuery.ts and another in unicodeLike.ts).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Two implementations that can drift, and the next consumer inherits neither — which is precisely IAC-2's requirement that the bound live inside `likePatternToRegex` so every consumer inherits it. v4's own review established this; it still holds with spending-spreadsheet.ts as a fourth consumer of `filterCategoriesByConditions`.

alternatives_considered.approach: Fail CLOSED on a refused pattern: return no match, so the axis drops every category.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It reintroduces the money bug fixed in PR #9. The axis would be narrower than the query's result set, so categories the query fetched would lose their money from every total. Verified against the source: returning 1 from unicodeLike keeps every outcome inside a subset of the full result set (`$like` matches everything, `$notlike` matches only NULL-column rows), so the axis is never narrower in either direction. This is also why the failure signal in AC-3 is a collapse to three rows rather than an empty table — the three synthetic rows render regardless.

alternatives_considered.approach: Remove the `OR left IS NULL` disjunct from `$notlike` in compiler.ts so that a refused doesNotContain really does match no transaction everywhere.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It would make the claim true by changing matching semantics for every `$notlike` query in the product, not just refused ones — rows with a NULL value in the filtered column would stop matching a `doesNotContain` rule that has always matched them. That is a behaviour change well outside this ticket, and it would break the existing assertion `notes is ''` -> ['4','5'] (transaction-rules.test.ts:586), which passes precisely because NULL and '' both satisfy that condition.

alternatives_considered.approach: Rewrite the pattern to remove ambiguity (e.g. make consecutive `%` collapse to one `.*`).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It changes matching semantics rather than bounding cost, and `%%%` already means 'match everything' and is pinned by existing tests in three files. It would still leave a `%` on each side of a long literal run. Out of the ticket's scope.

Length is a necessary guard but not a sufficient one — 8 wildcards in 9 characters is the pathological case that hangs, while a 254-character run of `x` costs nothing. Both bounds are needed, and AC-8 pins both.

Defensible on the measurement (3 ms vs 21 ms per category), but it would reject `contains '%'` and `contains '?'`, which both compile to exactly 3 — the boundary that three existing tests in budgetDataQuery.test.ts already pin. 4 is the smallest cap that leaves the accepted region provably untouched.

alternatives_considered.approach: Give unicodeLike its own NULL-aware refusal (return 0 when the value is NULL), so a refused doesNotContain matches no transaction on nullable columns too.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It would be a second, different refusal rule layered on top of the helper's, and it would change the accepted case as well: `unicodeLike('%', null)` currently returns 1 (there is an existing assertion for exactly that at unicodeLike.test.ts, 'should treat null value as empty string') and the `$notlike` disjunct is what makes NULL rows match. Making the refusal NULL-aware would couple the bound to a per-column property it has no business knowing about, and it would still leave the axis and the query disagreeing for any report filter on a category the user has left uncategorized.

alternatives_considered.approach: Have QA untick 'Show uncategorized' and 'Show off budget' to make an empty table observable, as an earlier review suggested.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Checked against the source and it would not work, so following it would produce a QA script that fails for the wrong reason. `filterHiddenItems` is applied to query data inside `recalculate`, while the rows themselves are built by mapping over `groupByList`, and `categoryLists` appends the three synthetic categories unconditionally (ReportOptions.ts:388-401). Un-ticking those toggles zeroes the synthetic rows' amounts but does not remove them, and with 'Show empty rows' ON they still render. The correct failure signal is a collapse to three rows.

alternatives_considered.approach: Use an ordinary filter value (such as `Food`) to record the QA reference row count, as an earlier plan did.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The action cannot produce the stated result. `contains Food` narrows the axis — `canNarrowAxisByConditions` returns true for a single non-OR category condition and `filterCategoriesByConditions` keeps only `%Food%` matches — so it yields 4 rows, not 21. The reference must be recorded with no filter applied.

alternatives_considered.approach: Use `%oo%` as the refused boundary value, as v5 did, describing it as 5 wildcards.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The value wraps to `%%oo%%`, which is 4 unescaped wildcards and would be ACCEPTED under this change — the QA step would report the wrong verdict on a correct build. `%%oo%` (wrapping to `%%%oo%%`, 5) is the value that crosses the cap; it is one character longer than the accepted-side `%%oo`, so the pair is adjacent in the input.

alternatives_considered.approach: Delete the `list === categories.list` identity shortcut at :151, as v5's file entry implied was safe.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is not dead code. `canNarrowAxisByConditions` returns true at :99-101 for any conjunction without examining fields, so a `notes`-only filter passes the gate, falls into the :192 early return, and the shortcut fires; the unsupported-condition fallback at :202 does the same. budgetDataQuery.test.ts:451-455 and :458-476 assert `toBe(axis)` for both, so removing it would break existing tests and change behaviour for a legitimate empty group in an unfiltered report.

validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: Every claim about the source was re-verified at HEAD (a596d04f) rather than carried from v6, and every wildcard and length figure comes from running the counter over the wrapped pattern — the failure mode that got v5 rejected, so the two boundary values in the QA script are one character apart and the implementer can re-derive them. The objection was checked against the source before being conceded: compiler.ts:741-743 does emit `OR left IS NULL`, `notes` is `f('string')` with no `required` in the AQL schema, the fixture does hold transaction '4' with `notes: null` at line 542, and '5' is `''` rather than NULL — so the split into two assertions is arithmetic, not interpretation. What is NOT verified end-to-end is the timing claim in a live browser against a large budget (the demo budget is too small to exhibit the hang), which is why AC-1 is written to what a browser can observe and AC-8 carries the falsifiable structural form. Confidence is a notch below v6 because the rules-side outcome is genuinely split by column nullability rather than being one clean statement, and that split has to survive a reviewer's reading of three separate assertions.
validated_work_order.debate_summary: The single objection against v6 is re-checked against the source at HEAD (a596d04f) rather than conceded from memory, and it is upheld in full. The claim it names — a refused `doesNotContain` matches no transaction — appeared in four places (risks[1], AC-10, AC-11, tests[2].cases[1], files[1].why) and is false as stated. `compiler.ts:741-743` emits `$notlike` as `(NOT UNICODE_LIKE(pat, NORMALISE(left)) OR left IS NULL)`; a refusal returns 1, so `NOT 1` is 0 and a row qualifies exactly when `left IS NULL`. That is 'no transaction' only for a non-nullable column, and every field `doesNotContain` accepts on the rules path is nullable: `notes` and `imported_payee` are `f('string')` with no `required` in the AQL schema, and `payee` resolves to `payees.name` through a LEFT JOIN. `notes` is also the field the existing sibling assertion at transaction-rules.test.ts:576 uses for `contains`, and the same fixture holds transaction '4' with `notes: null` at :542 while '5' is `''` — an empty string, not NULL — so a refused `notes doesNotContain` matches exactly ['4'] and a refused `payee doesNotContain` matches [] only because all five fixture rows happen to have a payee. Corrected everywhere it appeared: AC-10 now states the two operators separately (under `$like` every transaction including NULL-column rows; under `$notlike` exactly the NULL-column rows), AC-11 now requires all three assertions rather than one generalised claim, tests[2] splits into the two cases the objection asks for plus an instruction to sort the id lists (the fixture's query order is `['4','5','3']` for a payee filter, so insertion order was never the contract), and the proposed unicodeLike.ts comment is rewritten to carry the same qualified statement — it sits four lines above `return cachedRegExp.test(value) ? 1 : 0;`, so an unqualified version there would read as current. AC-10's sabotage check survives the split: flipping unicodeLike to return 0 for a refusal makes `payee doesNotContain` return all five rows instead of [] and `notes doesNotContain` return all five instead of ['4'], so both new assertions fail. Nothing about the safety argument moves — both outcomes are subsets of 'everything', so the axis is still never narrower than the query, which is the invariant PR #9 fixed. The objection's own note that the axis argument is unchanged is confirmed: budgetDataQuery.ts runs the pattern in JS over `CategoryEntity.name`, typed `string`, with no SQL NULL in play, so there the refusal genuinely does keep every category for both operators. Everything carried forward from v6 that this objection did not touch — the cap of 4 and its machine-derived boundary pair (`%%oo` accepted against `%%oo%` refused, one character apart), the unchanged accepted region (the largest value any existing test pins is 3), the bound living only inside `likePatternToRegex`, `doesNotContain` returning `true` on a null matcher, unicodeLike's `=== undefined` sentinel, the identity shortcut comment left alone with one added sentence, the demo-budget-too-small limitation — was re-verified against the source and stands.
evidence: packages/loot-core/src/shared/likePattern.ts:16 — `export function likePatternToRegex(pattern: string): RegExp` with no length or wildcard bound; :14 exports REGEX_SPECIAL; :25 carries the `// ? added here` scar.

packages/loot-core/src/server/aql/compiler.ts:733-735 — `$like` emits `UNICODE_LIKE(<normalised pattern>, NORMALISE(<left>))`, no NULL disjunct. :741-743 — `$notlike` emits `(NOT UNICODE_LIKE(<normalised pattern>, NORMALISE(<left>)) OR <left> IS NULL)`. A refusal returning 1 therefore makes `$notlike` reduce to `left IS NULL`.

packages/loot-core/src/server/aql/schema/index.ts:44 — `notes: f('string')` with no `required`, so notes is nullable; :46 `imported_payee: f('string')` likewise. `payees.name` is `required: true` but is reached from transactions by LEFT JOIN (compiler.ts), so a transaction with no payee yields NULL there too.

packages/loot-core/src/server/transactions/transaction-rules.test.ts:498-552 — the 'transactions can be queried by rule' fixture: '1' notes 'barr', '2' 'fooo', '3' 'FooO', '4' notes null (:542), '5' notes '' — all five have a payee (kroger or lowes). :576 is the sibling `notes contains 'oo'` -> ['2','3'] assertion; :586 `notes is ''` -> ['4','5'] confirms '' and NULL are distinct rows here.

packages/loot-core/src/server/transactions/transaction-rules.ts:645-663 — `contains` compiles to `$like` on `'%' + value + '%'` and `doesNotContain` to `$notlike` on the same wrap; `apply` adds a `$lower` transform for string-typed fields, so `notes` reaches the disjunct as `UNICODE_LOWER(notes) IS NULL` (index.ts:281 registers it as `arg => arg?.toLowerCase()`, so NULL stays NULL).

packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/unicodeLike.ts:11-20 — `if (!value) value = ''` coerces a NULL row value to '', the LRU is `LRUCache<string, RegExp>` and the presence test is `if (!cachedRegExp)`, which would treat a cached `null` as a miss.

files.change: Add two module-private constants, `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH = 256` and `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS = 4`. Change the signature to `export function likePatternToRegex(pattern: string): RegExp | null`. Return `null` when `pattern.length > MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH` before compiling anything. Inside the existing loop, add an `unescapedWildcards` counter incremented only on the unescaped `%` and `?` branches (never on the escaped branch, so `\%` costs 0 and `%\%%` costs 2) and `return null` once it exceeds the cap. Extend the module doc comment with the contract — a `null` means 'this pattern is refused, it was not compiled', and consumers must fail OPEN (keep every row, or keep every axis category) rather than closed, because the report axis may never be narrower than the query's result set — and record why the cap is 4 by pointing at the measured curve from the epic (3 wildcards 3 ms per category, 4 -> 21 ms, 5 -> 150 ms, 6 -> 850 ms, and the axis predicate runs once per category per condition on every render; 200 compiles of one pattern total under a millisecond, so the cost is all in `.test()` and memoisation cannot fix it). Delete `export` from `REGEX_SPECIAL` (no consumers outside this file) and delete the `// ? added here` scar on the escaped-wildcard line, keeping `// escaped wildcard - treat as literal character`.
files.why: This is the single definition of the LIKE pattern language that `UNICODE_LIKE` speaks, so a bound placed here is inherited by every consumer rather than re-implemented at each — which is what IAC-2 asks for. Returning `RegExp | null` instead of a `RegExp` makes the refusal direction a compile-time obligation at each call site instead of a silent default.

files.change: Retype the LRU to `LRUCache<string, RegExp | null>` so a refusal is cacheable. Replace the `if (!cachedRegExp)` presence test with `=== undefined` — `null` is a legitimate cached value and the old falsy test would treat a cached refusal as a miss and recompile once per scanned row, which is the opposite of the point. On a cache miss, store whatever `likePatternToRegex` returned, `null` included; on a hit that is `null`, return 1 immediately, keeping the `if (!value) value = ''` coercion above it so a NULL row still takes the refusal path rather than short-circuiting. Write a comment immediately above that `return 1` stating the direction in the compiler's terms, NOT as a universal: refusing returns 1, so under `$like` (compiler.ts:733-735, no NULL disjunct) every transaction matches including rows whose column is NULL, and under `$notlike` (compiler.ts:741-743, `(NOT UNICODE_LIKE(...) OR left IS NULL)`) `NOT 1` is 0 and a row qualifies exactly when its column IS NULL — no rows for a non-nullable column, the NULL-valued rows for a nullable one such as `notes`. Say in the comment that both are subsets of the full result set, which is what keeps the report axis from becoming narrower than the query.
files.why: This is the SQL `$like` / `$notlike` path compiled in packages/loot-core/src/server/aql/compiler.ts:733-743, and it is registered as the `UNICODE_LIKE` SQLite function by BOTH backends (index.electron.ts:158 and index.ts:283), so it is reached from the desktop Electron app, the browser app, the API and the sync server. Returning 1 is what keeps the report axis from becoming narrower than the query's result set. The comment has to carry the qualification because the unqualified version ('a refused doesNotContain matches none') is false for every nullable column the rules path allows, and a reader four lines above `return cachedRegExp.test(value) ? 1 : 0;` would otherwise take it as current.

qa_script: Start the app (`yarn start`), open it, and choose 'Don't use a server' then 'View demo' on the initial setup screen. Use the demo budget, NOT 'Start budgeting' — 'View demo' runs createTestBudget (mocks/budget.ts:746), which creates 16 categories in 3 groups (8 Usual Expenses, 5 Bills, 3 Income). Open Reports > Custom report.

SETUP — create two categories, so the escaped-wildcard steps below have something to narrow to. Go to the Budget page and hover any category group in the left sidebar; click the 'Add category' button (aria-label 'Add category', SidebarGroup.tsx:176) and type `50% off`, which saves as you type; press Escape. Do the same and type `C_Sharp`. This leaves 18 categories. Skip this step only to confirm the negative case: without it, `\%` and `_` correctly narrow to the three synthetic rows, which is why a previous plan's assertion could not distinguish that from the bug.

In the Custom report sidebar turn ON 'Show empty rows' (ReportSidebar.tsx:494). It is required for every count below — `filterEmptyRows` returns `!showEmpty ? showHide : true` (filterEmptyRows.ts:24) — so with it off, empty rows are hidden and the axis cannot be observed. Leave Split on its default 'Category'. Do NOT untick 'Show uncategorized' or 'Show off budget' to look for an empty table: those toggle transaction data, not axis rows.

REFERENCE — record the baseline with NO filter applied: do not add a filter row yet (a filter row with its value cleared is equivalent). Record the exact row list and count, and the total. With the 18-category budget and Split:Category this is 21 rows — the 18 categories plus Uncategorized, Off budget and Transfers, which `categoryLists` appends unconditionally (ReportOptions.ts:388-401). Every later step is compared against this. Do NOT use an ordinary value such as `Food` for the reference: `contains Food` NARROWS the axis to Food alone and yields 4 rows, which is not the reference.

ACCEPTED SIDE, ordinary — add a filter row (field `Category`, condition `contains`) and type `oo`. This compiles to the pattern `%oo%` (2 unescaped wildcards) and must be accepted. The axis narrows to Food alone plus the three synthetic rows: 4 rows, total for Food only.

ACCEPTED BOUNDARY — replace the value with `%%oo`. As a `contains` value this wraps to the pattern `%%%oo%`, which is exactly 4 unescaped wildcards, and must be accepted. Expect 4 rows (Food plus the three synthetic). If the axis stays at 21, the cap is not 4. Two neighbouring values that would NOT test this: `%oo` wraps to `%%oo%`, only 3 wildcards, and `%oo%` wraps to `%%oo%%`, also only 4 — the value that crosses the cap is the one with a third trailing `%`, below.

REFUSED BOUNDARY — replace the value with `%%oo%`. This wraps to `%%%oo%%`, exactly 5 unescaped wildcards, and must be refused. The axis keeps EVERY category: 21 rows, the same total as step 4. Three rows here means fail-closed. Note the contrast with the previous step: the two values differ by a single character, so this pair pins the cap at exactly 4 rather than merely somewhere below 5.

HEAVY WILDCARD — replace the value with `%%%%%%Z` (wraps to 8 wildcards). Same expectation: 21 rows, unchanged total, page responsive the whole time. If the row count collapses to 3 (Uncategorized / Off budget / Transfers, all 0.00), the refusal direction is wrong. Switch Split to Group and repeat: correct is 4 rows (3 groups plus Uncategorized & Off budget); a collapse to 1 means fail-closed.

OPERATOR MIRROR — change the condition to `does not contain`, leaving the value at `%%%%%%Z`. The axis must again keep all 21 rows. This is the direction that reintroduces the money bug if it is implemented as a negated match-everything: the symptom is a collapse to 3 rows, with the report totals reading 0.00 while transactions clearly exist. Note what this step does NOT show: the rules-side `$notlike` outcome for a refused pattern depends on whether the column is NULL (AC-11), which a category name never is on the axis — so 21 rows here is the correct and only expected result.

ESCAPED WILDCARDS — back to `contains`. `\%` wraps to `%\%%`, only 2 wildcards because the escaped one is a literal, and must narrow to exactly `50% off` plus the three synthetic rows (4 rows). `_` must narrow to exactly `C_Sharp` plus three (4 rows) — one survivor proves `_` is a literal and not a SQL wildcard, since a real SQL `_` would have kept all 18. `50\% off` narrows to exactly `50% off`. `?` narrows to all 21 (wraps to 3 wildcards, inside the cap). `%` narrows to all 21 (also 3).
NEGATIVE CONTROLS — `oo` keeps only Food (4 rows). `Food` keeps only Food (4 rows). These confirm ordinary values are untouched by the bound.

LENGTH BOUND — paste a value of 255 characters. Wrapped pattern length 257, refused by length. The axis must show the full 21 rows again, the same total as step 4. Then paste 254 characters: wrapped pattern length exactly 256, ACCEPTED, and because no category name contains that run of characters it narrows to the THREE SYNTHETIC ROWS. State this plainly rather than treating it as a pass or a failure: those three rows are byte-for-byte what a fail-closed build renders, so the 254-character observation CANNOT falsify the refusal direction. What the pair (255 chars -> 21 rows, 254 chars -> 3 rows) does establish is that the length bound exists and sits exactly between two adjacent input lengths. What pins acceptance at exactly 256 characters is AC-8's unit test, not this step.
RELOAD — press F5 with the report still open, and re-enter `%%%%%%Z`. Same 21 rows. This rules out a stale-bundle illusion.

CONSOLE — with the devtools console open, clear it, then step through 8, 9 and 12. No `pageerror` and no unhandled rejection. Console noise from dev-mode (HMR, plugin service) is expected and is not a failure.
residual_risks: The demo budget is too small to exhibit the original hang, so QA cannot confirm the seconds-to-minutes freeze directly; it can only confirm the axis stays open and the UI stays responsive. The magnitude claim rests on the epic's measured curve (recorded in the likePattern.ts doc comment) plus AC-8's structural test, not on the browser run.

A user on a budget with thousands of categories who currently relies on a 5-wildcard value will see it silently stop filtering — and in a transaction rule, silently start matching every transaction under `contains`, or under `doesNotContain` silently match only the transactions with an empty/NULL value in that field. That is the intended trade (5 wildcards is 150 ms per category at the epic's measurement and grows from there) but it is a silent behaviour change on both surfaces, which is why the release note says a refused pattern keeps every category rather than dropping them, and why the QA script exercises the accepted side (`%%oo`, exactly 4 wildcards) alongside the refused side.

The rules-side outcome of a refused `doesNotContain` is data-dependent, so a user reading a rule's effect after this change may see it match a small set of NULL-valued rows rather than the empty set they would predict from the axis behaviour on reports. The two surfaces genuinely differ, and AC-11 plus the unicodeLike.ts comment are where that difference is recorded; it is not resolvable by making them agree without changing matching semantics, which is out of scope.
risks: The refusal direction is the money invariant. A fail-closed slip in budgetDataQuery.ts or unicodeLike.ts reintroduces the defect class fixed in PR #9, and it is invisible in a small budget because the categories it drops have no money. Mitigated by AC-9 and AC-10 (test) and by the mirror case in custom-spreadsheet.test.ts asserting the totals, not just the row count.

The transaction-rules direction is a silent behaviour change on a path this ticket does not otherwise touch, and the two operators do NOT invert symmetrically. After this change a `contains` rule whose value the bound refuses matches EVERY transaction, and a `doesNotContain` rule whose value is refused matches exactly the rows whose column IS NULL — every transaction for a non-nullable column, only the NULL-valued rows for a nullable one such as `notes`. That is the open direction the report's money invariant requires, applied consistently, but it is worth naming because a rule that used to apply to a handful of payees would now apply to all of them. AC-11 pins all three cases and the change is bounded by the fact that a value with five or more unescaped wildcards already matched almost everything before it.

The LRU sentinel. Reusing the existing `if (!cachedRegExp)` with a nullable value would treat a cached `null` as a miss and recompile per row — correctness-neutral but a per-row compile cost on exactly the pattern that is already slow to evaluate. AC-10 pins it.

No forbidden path is touched: `.sdlc/memory/**`, `docs/spec/**`, `docs/prd.md`, `docs/trd.md`, `docs/ui.md`, `.github/**` and `.sdlc/**` are all outside files[]. The only non-source file created is a release note under upcoming-release-notes/, which the CI gate requires.
No non-allowlisted host is required: the change is local code and unit tests, and QA runs against `yarn start` on localhost only.

The one-sentence addition to the :148-153 comment is a behavioural claim that is easy to get backwards. It must say the lists hold the same CONTENTS but are new arrays, that a refusal is not one of the identity early returns, and that an already-empty group is therefore dropped; stating that the identity shortcut can never fire would be false (AC-12) and would make a correct implementation look wrong to a later reader.

The comment written into unicodeLike.ts is the highest-risk prose in this diff, because it sits four lines above `return cachedRegExp.test(value) ? 1 : 0;` and a reader will take it as current. Writing 'a refused doesNotContain matches no transaction' there would be false for every nullable column the rules path allows, which is precisely the error this version corrects. AC-10 states the qualified form the comment must carry.
validated_work_order.root_cause: `likePatternToRegex` compiles an unbounded number of `%`/`?` wildcards into a single regex source, so the regex engine's backtracking cost grows exponentially with the wildcard count and a user's filter value becomes a denial-of-service vector on the report category axis and on the SQL `$like` path. There is no bound anywhere in the pattern language definition, and because every consumer calls the same helper, none of them has a place to express a limit of its own.

returns null for a pattern of five unescaped wildcards and compiles one of exactly four ('%%%%' accepted, '%%%%%' refused) — the boundary pair, 4 against 5
returns null for a pattern longer than 256 characters and compiles one of exactly 256
does not count backslash-escaped wildcards toward the limit: 'a\%b' and '50\% off' compile with 0 counted wildcards, and the wrapped contains value '\%' (pattern '%\%%') compiles with 2
returns 1 for a refused pattern, so a $like filter keeps every transaction including one whose column is NULL (unicodeLike(refused, null) is 1)
keeps returning 1 for a refused pattern without recompiling it per row (falsified by reverting the === undefined sentinel to !cachedRegExp)
still returns 1 for accepted all-wildcard patterns such as %%% and %?% (3 wildcards, inside the cap)
a contains rule whose value is refused by the wildcard bound matches EVERY transaction through the compiled $like filter — all five fixture rows, including '4' whose notes is NULL

a doesNotContain rule whose value is refused matches the transactions whose column IS NULL and no others: on the `notes` field, exactly ['4'] (notes NULL), because $notlike is compiled as (NOT UNICODE_LIKE(...) OR left IS NULL) and the refusal returns 1 so NOT 1 is 0

the same refused doesNotContain on a field that is non-nullable across the fixture returns no transaction at all: on `payee` (which resolves to payees.name by LEFT JOIN and every fixture row has a payee), [] — this is the pair that pins the direction, since the two fields differ only in whether any row's column is NULL

assert the transaction id lists SORTED, not in the order the query happens to return them (the existing assertions in this fixture return ['4','5','3'] for a payee filter, so insertion order is not the contract)
a contains rule whose value is refused by the length bound (255 characters, wrapped pattern 257) behaves the same as one refused by the wildcard bound
an ordinary contains rule is unaffected: a value with few wildcards still narrows as before, so the sibling `notes contains 'oo'` -> ['2','3'] assertion keeps its meaning
contains with a refused value keeps every category in the axis (value '%%oo%' -> pattern %%%oo%%, 5 wildcards)

doesNotContain with a refused value keeps every category in the axis — the direction that would drop every category if implemented as a negated match-everything; the axis runs in JS over CategoryEntity.name, so unlike the rules path no IS NULL disjunct is in play and there is nothing to exclude
contains with exactly four unescaped wildcards ('%%oo' -> %%%oo%) still narrows the axis, and five ('%%oo%') does not — the boundary pair

doesNotContain with a refused value renders every fetched category
a contains condition whose value is refused produces an $oneof over every category, a superset of the query result rather than a subset

validated_work_order.understanding:
`likePatternToRegex` (packages/loot-core/src/shared/likePattern.ts:16) turns every unescaped `%` into `.*` and every unescaped `?` into `.` with no limit, so a user-supplied filter value compiles into a regex whose `.test()` backtracks catastrophically against real names — the epic measured 3 wildcards at 3ms per category, 4 at 21ms, 5 at 150ms, 6 at 850ms, and the axis predicate runs once per category per condition on every render. The bound belongs where the pattern language is defined so every consumer inherits it, and the refusal DIRECTION is the substance: the report's money invariant (PR #9) requires the axis never to be narrower than the query's result set, so a refused pattern must fail OPEN.

This version answers the one objection raised against v6, which is upheld and corrected throughout.

**Objection — 'a refused doesNotContain matches NO transaction' is false for a nullable column.** The v6 plan stated it in risks[1], acceptance[9] (AC-10), acceptance[10] (AC-11), tests[2].cases[1] and files[1].why. compiler.ts:741-743 emits `$notlike` as `(NOT UNICODE_LIKE(pat, NORMALISE(left)) OR left IS NULL)`. unicodeLike returns 1 on a refusal, so `NOT 1` is 0 and a row qualifies exactly when `left IS NULL` — which is 'no transaction' only when `left` is non-nullable. On the rules path `left` is a nullable column for every field `doesNotContain` accepts: `notes` (AQL schema `notes: f('string')`, no `required`), `imported_payee` likewise, and `payee` resolves to `payees.name` reached by LEFT JOIN, so a transaction with no payee is NULL there too.

Concretely, on the existing fixture in transaction-rules.test.ts ('transactions can be queried by rule', transactions '1'-'5'): `notes` is NULL only for transaction '4' (test line 542), while '1'/'2'/'3' are strings and '5' is `''` — an empty string, not NULL. `notes` is also the field the sibling assertion at line 576 already uses for `contains`. So a refused `notes doesNotContain` matches exactly ['4'], not []. A refused `payee doesNotContain` matches [] only because all five fixture rows happen to have a payee.

Corrected, and this is the whole shape of the fix's contract: on the rules/query side a refusal returns 1, which means `$like` matches EVERY transaction (including rows whose column is NULL) and `$notlike` matches EXACTLY THE ROWS WHOSE COLUMN IS NULL — a strict subset of everything, never a superset. Both directions stay inside 'a subset of what the axis kept', so the money invariant holds and nothing in the plan's safety argument changes. The axis side is unaffected and the objection says so: budgetDataQuery.ts runs the pattern in JS over `CategoryEntity.name` (typed `string`, and no SQL NULL is in play), so `doesNotContain` there must return `true` on a null matcher and keeps every category. This version states the qualified claim everywhere it previously stated the false universal, makes the proposed unicodeLike.ts comment say the qualified thing rather than 'matches none', and splits tests[2].cases[1] into the two assertions the objection asks for (a non-nullable-in-this-fixture field -> [], `notes` -> the NULL rows). AC-10's sabotage check survives the split: flipping unicodeLike to return 0 for a refusal makes `payee doesNotContain` return all five rows instead of [] and `notes doesNotContain` return all five instead of ['4'], so both new assertions fail.

Every number in this plan comes from running the wildcard counter (the loop that will live in likePattern.ts, incrementing only on the unescaped `%` and `?` branches and skipping the escape branch) over the wrapped pattern, not from hand-counting — that hand-counting error is what got v5 rejected. Measured through the `contains` wrap `'%' + value + '%'`:

  value `oo`      -> `%oo%`       len 4   wildcards=2  ACCEPTED
  value `%oo`     -> `%%oo%`      len 5   wildcards=3  ACCEPTED
  value `%%oo`    -> `%%%oo%`     len 6   wildcards=4  ACCEPTED  <- accepted boundary
  value `%oo%`    -> `%%oo%%`     len 6   wildcards=4  ACCEPTED
  value `%%oo%`   -> `%%%oo%%`    len 7   wildcards=5  REFUSED   <- refused boundary
  value `%%%%%%Z` -> `%%%%%%%Z%`  len 9   wildcards=8  REFUSED
  value `%`       -> `%%%`        len 3   wildcards=3  ACCEPTED
  value `?`       -> `%?%`        len 3   wildcards=3  ACCEPTED
  value `o%`      -> `%o%%`       len 4   wildcards=3  ACCEPTED
  value `\%`      -> `%\%%`       len 4   wildcards=2  ACCEPTED  (the middle one is escaped)
  value `_`       -> `%_%`        len 3   wildcards=2  ACCEPTED
  value `50\% off`-> `%50\% off%` len 10  wildcards=2  ACCEPTED
  value `x`*254   -> len 256      ACCEPTED by length
  value `x`*255   -> len 257      REFUSED  by length

Raw patterns: `%%%%` = 4 accepted, `%%%%%` = 5 refused, `a\%b` = 0, `50\% off` = 0. The largest value ANY existing test pins is 3 (`contains '%'`, `contains '?'`, `contains 'o%'`), machine-checked across budgetDataQuery.test.ts, custom-spreadsheet.test.ts and unicodeLike.test.ts, so a cap of 4 leaves every existing assertion's meaning untouched. The boundary pair for QA is `%%oo` (4, accepted, narrows to Food) against `%%oo%` (5, refused, keeps all 21) — adjacent in the input, one character apart.

Carried forward unchanged from v6 because it was not objected to and was re-verified at HEAD (a596d04f): the bound lives inside `likePatternToRegex` and nowhere else; `doesNotContain` on the axis must return `true` on a null matcher rather than negate a match-everything; the identity shortcut at budgetDataQuery.ts:151 CAN still fire once a condition is being evaluated (canNarrowAxisByConditions returns true at :99-101 for any conjunction without checking fields, so a `notes`-only filter reaches the :192 early return), the existing tests pin that by `toBe(axis)`, and the comments at :115-125 and :148-153 are therefore left alone with one added sentence; unicodeLike's `=== undefined` sentinel; the demo-budget-too-small limitation on AC-1.
unknowns: Whether normalising before counting can change a pattern's length across the 256 boundary: `getNormalisedString` maps ß to ss and œ to oe, so a value of 254 ß characters normalises past 256 and is refused. This is the conservative direction and, per the assumption above, both call paths normalise identically, so the axis and the query still agree. It is a note for a maintainer rather than a risk to this change.
Whether any non-English locale normalises a category name to characters that change the wildcard count. No such mapping exists in normalisation.ts today, so this is likewise a maintenance note.

Whether a user reads the rules-side outcome of a refused `doesNotContain` as a bug. It is a genuine semantic change on that surface, recorded in AC-11 and in the unicodeLike.ts comment, but no UI distinguishes 'refused' from 'matched nothing', so a user has no signal that the pattern was refused rather than evaluated. Surfacing one is a product decision this ticket does not make (see out_of_scope).
